Finance Betting games · the coin flip

Betting everything makes the average rich and almost every player poor

A thousand players take the same bet a hundred times: a fair coin, +50% on heads, −40% on tails. On average each round adds 5%, yet staking it all leaves the typical player with half a penny on the pound. A smaller stake, or sharing the luck, turns the same coin into growth for nearly everyone.

Quick build: fewer trials, so the ranks in stage 2 are noisy. Rebuild without --quick for the real figures.
1 · All in

Everyone stakes all they have, every round.

The average climbs while the typical player sinks

2 · One Kelly player

A 1001st player stakes a quarter of their wealth each round, with coins of their own.

3 · Everyone sensible

Every player stakes Kelly alone, or the table pools its luck and shares it, at the Kelly stake or all in.

4 · A mixed table

A quarter of each: a pool of 250 all in, a pool of 250 at Kelly, 250 all in alone, 250 Kelly alone.

What Kelly does not promise

Fair play

Every stake is chosen before the coin is flipped, from the public terms of the bet and what that player has seen so far. The outcomes are drawn in advance only so that every scheme faces the same luck; no strategy can see them. This is tested: two tables that agree on everything a player has seen must give that player the same stakes, whatever the other players' coins or the flips still to come.
